* applying kernels to annealed distributions e.g. annealed importance sampling

My guess is that while this is non-trivial - it can be done by "simply" writing R or python wrappers for a bunch of underlying functions.  Any thoughts?  Is this a common request (sorry if I missed it).

Cheers,
David

If the recomputed lp__ depends on the continuous unknown y, then HMC would need to know the derivative of that with respect to y. And that would basically entail working out the derivative analytically and writing custom C++. Moreover, Stan currently has a really hard distinction between known data (that never changes) and unknown parameters (that it updates). So, there is not a mechanism by which you can pass "data" that is really an unknown that gets updated some other way.

Ben

parts:
My hope was primarily to deal with models changing dimension and with discrete latent variables...   but I put in a couple of other suggestions ...  (I agree the annealing bit is particularly questionable)...  On the other hand Mark Girolami actually recommends interweaving here: http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/publications/PAPERS/9382/tech_rep_lgms.pdf .  Iain Murray argues running HMC on the full posterior for latent variable Gaussian process hierarchical  models doesn't work so well - but I must admit I don't understand why.

It is fairly common that a published algorithm uses HMC as a kernel in combination with standard Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs kernels...  it would be surprising if this were _never_ a good idea....   It would really be wonderful to be able to use Stan to make the HMC part easier...  but it looks like that is at least not easy right now...  although I am still a little puzzled as to why...

Thanks again, for the feed back and for Stan!

Well, if it matters at all I work for Mark, so I'm not coming from an orthogonal direction!

Firstly, the big issue here is sampling jointly or sampling conditionally.  Sampling conditionally is always going to bring in problems when the target measure has large correlations, i.e. any realistic problem.  HMC appears to use a Gibbs step to sample the auxiliary momenta, but technically that sampling is doing something else.  Ignoring the technical details, HMC is making a joint update of all the model parameters which is what is important.  

This leaves two issues: hierarchical modes are hard and discrete models are harder.

We review hierarchical models thoroughly in http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906, in particular we address why Euclidean HMC can run into problems.  A common approach that people take, starting with Radford Neal way back when he was first introducing HMC into stats, is to sample from the hyperparameters conditional on the local parameters,
but this inevitably leads to large autocorrelations because of the strong dependencies between the hyperparameters and the local parameters.  What you'd really want to do is sample from the marginal distribution of the hyperparameters, but computing that distribution is a tremendously difficult task.  Pseudomarginal methods are trying to solve this, but they are hard to make general and can run into their own pathologies.  As noted in the paper, Riemannian HMC solves many of these problems by construction, and it's coming soon to Stan.  At the moment your best bet is to find a good non-centered parameterization.

Everyone wants discrete parameters but everyone also needs to understand the underlying problems.  Without the nice structure of a continuous measure, it's very, very hard to construct an efficient sampler.  Moreover, if you split your parameters into continuous and discrete then you're doing conditional updates, which will be slow as discussed above.  We've seen lots of success when the discrete parameters can be marginalized out to give a fully continuous model amenable to HMC.  This includes discrete latent models, provided there aren't too many possible states.

You can certainly use Stan as a sampling API and stick it into a bigger sampler, but without addressing the fundamental problems with discrete variables and conditional updates you're only going to be able to go so far.

I'm not a stan user, but I have implemented NUTS together with other samplers, particularly DREAM (and RWM). The reason is two-fold - DREAM can handle, at least to some degree, discrete parameters and multi-modal situations. Secondly, when DREAM works well, it works well, and can be faster than NUTS. So I mix randomly DREAM and NUTS, in concept NUTS is used to generate a good population, and then DREAM is used to sample and difference from that population. This is all done randomly at each step and for each chain.
 
This also avoids one of the main pitfalls of DREAM, IMHO, that heuristic tricks have to be used to make it go outside of the hyperplane defined by the chains at the current step. The inclusion of NUTS means that those tricks are no longer needed.
 
In addition, I examine the acceptance rate for DREAM, and vary the proportion of time spent in DREAM according to how close the acceptance rate is to the theoretical value for normal distributions. I use dual averaging for the DREAM step (i.e. the scaled difference).
 
Remarkably, the dual averaging generated a step size almost identical to the theoretical value for a normal test problem. Well, I'm always surprised when theory meets practice.
 
So, long story short, I found value in mixing samplers. It's the same when you mix optimisation algorithms, they all have different good and bad behaviours, and a mixture is more robust.

Bob, I'm afraid I don't know exactly what you mean by 'ensemble' and 'interweaving'. But maybe this will help:
 
- I use multiple chains (8, for no particular reason), and parallelise at the likelihood function level, not the chain level. So I loop over steps, and for each step I loop over chains. I choose at random (with sampler weights) for each step/chain what sampler I am using, so for a given step there are multiple samplers, and of course the NUTS sampler takes a lot longer than the DREAM sampler, but that is OK because of the way I parallelise. It would be hopeless if I parallelised at the chain level.
 
- there are several different versions of DREAM. Some sample from other chains at the same step, others sample from a store of previous steps (DREAMZ). I use both methods. In pure DREAM, the problem with sampling from other chains is the one I mentioned, getting stuck in the same hyperplane, and they have various methods to overcome this, none of which I like. They are Gibbs-like, which is hopeless if the likelihood is not aligned with the axes. But by combining with NUTS, this problem is avoided. All the complexity of DREAM (choosing subsets of parameters, adding in a bit of random walk) can be avoided.
 
- I have a feeling, and it is no more than that, that DREAM sampling from other chains has a more satisfactory detailed balance proof, hence why I use multiple chains. But I may be wrong. the 'proofs' in DREAM are rather sketchy.
 
- whether the DREAM family, or my combined approach, strictly obey the necessary rules, is not something I am qualified to discuss. But in my tests they successfully reproduce the analytical results for complex high dimensional problems, which is more than good enough for my audience.
 
- speed and performance is critical in my application, it is an interactive tool for engineers which repeats MC many times, so I have to make some compromises to get the performance. Whether the compromises are real or imaginary I don't know (see above!), but without performance nobody would use it.
 
My video http://www.youtube.com/channel/UCQbRkgaevt0TSDzipvmtMKQ
 
shows, for EssRisk64DNormal, this combined approach for a 64 dimensional multivariate normal. In this case I have one chain, and DREAM samples from the store. Blue jumps are DREAM, green jumps are NUTS.
 
For the Haario problem (64 dimensional, each pair of parameters is a 2D Haario function, so it is much harder than the published function) DREAM works much less well, for obvious reasons. But my algorithm can recognise this, and adjust the amount of DREAM usage accordingly.
 
In concept, I guess you could say NUTS does the exploration, and other samplers fill in the gaps.
 
Also, when you combine samplers, you may need to look at modifying the algorithms for the individual samples, as I did for DREAM.  This is just the same when, for example, you combine evolutionary algorithm optimisers with local gradient optimisers - just plugging the two together is not a satisfactory solution, they have influence on each other, and opportunities also.
 
I really must look at Goodman-Weare in more detail one day.

Everyone wants discrete parameters but everyone also needs to understand the underlying problems.  Without the nice structure of a continuous measure, it's very, very hard to construct an efficient sampler.  Moreover, if you split your parameters into continuous and discrete then you're doing conditional updates, which will be slow as discussed above.  We've seen lots of success when the discrete parameters can be marginalized out to give a fully continuous model amenable to HMC.  This includes discrete latent models, provided there aren't too many possible states.

You can certainly use Stan as a sampling API and stick it into a bigger sampler, but without addressing the fundamental problems with discrete variables and conditional updates you're only going to be able to go so far.

Well, if it matters at all I work for Mark, so I'm not coming from an orthogonal direction!

Firstly, the big issue here is sampling jointly or sampling conditionally.  Sampling conditionally is always going to bring in problems when the target measure has large correlations, i.e. any realistic problem.  HMC appears to use a Gibbs step to sample the auxiliary momenta, but technically that sampling is doing something else.  Ignoring the technical details, HMC is making a joint update of all the model parameters which is what is important.  

This leaves two issues: hierarchical modes are hard and discrete models are harder.

We review hierarchical models thoroughly in http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906, in particular we address why Euclidean HMC can run into problems.  A common approach that people take, starting with Radford Neal way back when he was first introducing HMC into stats, is to sample from the hyperparameters conditional on the local parameters,
but this inevitably leads to large autocorrelations because of the strong dependencies between the hyperparameters and the local parameters.  What you'd really want to do is sample from the marginal distribution of the hyperparameters, but computing that distribution is a tremendously difficult task.  Pseudomarginal methods are trying to solve this, but they are hard to make general and can run into their own pathologies.  As noted in the paper, Riemannian HMC solves many of these problems by construction, and it's coming soon to Stan.  At the moment your best bet is to find a good non-centered parameterization.

Everyone wants discrete parameters but everyone also needs to understand the underlying problems.  Without the nice structure of a continuous measure, it's very, very hard to construct an efficient sampler.  Moreover, if you split your parameters into continuous and discrete then you're doing conditional updates, which will be slow as discussed above.  We've seen lots of success when the discrete parameters can be marginalized out to give a fully continuous model amenable to HMC.  This includes discrete latent models, provided there aren't too many possible states.

You can certainly use Stan as a sampling API and stick it into a bigger sampler, but without addressing the fundamental problems with discrete variables and conditional updates you're only going to be able to go so far.

Well, if it matters at all I work for Mark, so I'm not coming from an orthogonal direction!

Firstly, the big issue here is sampling jointly or sampling conditionally.  Sampling conditionally is always going to bring in problems when the target measure has large correlations, i.e. any realistic problem.  HMC appears to use a Gibbs step to sample the auxiliary momenta, but technically that sampling is doing something else.  Ignoring the technical details, HMC is making a joint update of all the model parameters which is what is important.  

This leaves two issues: hierarchical modes are hard and discrete models are harder.

We review hierarchical models thoroughly in http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906, in particular we address why Euclidean HMC can run into problems.  A common approach that people take, starting with Radford Neal way back when he was first introducing HMC into stats, is to sample from the hyperparameters conditional on the local parameters,
but this inevitably leads to large autocorrelations because of the strong dependencies between the hyperparameters and the local parameters.  What you'd really want to do is sample from the marginal distribution of the hyperparameters, but computing that distribution is a tremendously difficult task.  Pseudomarginal methods are trying to solve this, but they are hard to make general and can run into their own pathologies.  As noted in the paper, Riemannian HMC solves many of these problems by construction, and it's coming soon to Stan.  At the moment your best bet is to find a good non-centered parameterization.

Everyone wants discrete parameters but everyone also needs to understand the underlying problems.  Without the nice structure of a continuous measure, it's very, very hard to construct an efficient sampler.  Moreover, if you split your parameters into continuous and discrete then you're doing conditional updates, which will be slow as discussed above.  We've seen lots of success when the discrete parameters can be marginalized out to give a fully continuous model amenable to HMC.  This includes discrete latent models, provided there aren't too many possible states.

You can certainly use Stan as a sampling API and stick it into a bigger sampler, but without addressing the fundamental problems with discrete variables and conditional updates you're only going to be able to go so far.
